title: Knowing God as Father.  Part 1
scripture_text: “Watch out! Don’t do your good deeds publicly, to be admired by others, for you will lose the reward from your Father in heaven. When you give to someone in need, don’t do as the hypocrites do—blowing trumpets in the synagogues and streets to call attention to their acts of charity! I tell you the truth, they have received all the reward they will ever get. But when you give to someone in need, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand is doing. Give your gifts in private, and your Father, who sees everything, will reward you.
devotional:
“When you pray, don’t be like the hypocrites who love to pray publicly on street corners and in the synagogues where everyone can see them. I tell you the truth, that is all the reward they will ever get. But when you pray, go away by yourself, shut the door behind you, and pray to your Father in private. Then your Father, who sees everything, will reward you. “When you pray, don’t babble on and on as the Gentiles do. They think their prayers are answered merely by repeating their words again and again. Don’t be like them, for your Father knows exactly what you need even before you ask him! Pray like this: Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. May your Kingdom come soon. May your will be done on earth, as it is in heaven. Give us today the food we need and forgive us our sins, as we have forgiven those who sin against us. And don’t let us yield to temptation, but rescue us from the evil one. “If you forgive those who sin against you, your heavenly Father will forgive you. But if you refuse to forgive others, your Father will not forgive your sins.

“And when you fast, don’t make it obvious, as the hypocrites do, for they try to look miserable and dishevelled so people will admire them for their fasting. I tell you the truth, that is the only reward they will ever get. But when you fast, comb your hair and wash your face. Then no one will notice that you are fasting, except your Father, who knows what you do in private. And your Father, who sees everything, will reward you.

Matthew 6 begins with two very important words, which are “Be careful,’ [watch out NLT]. It would be tempting to just read over these two words and miss what they are saying. “Be Careful is one word in the Greek, PROSECHO. It means to “be continually guarding against.” It has the idea of continually watching yourself. It was used to describe the skill of a sea captain who was able to bring his vessel into harbour without beaching it on the hidden shallow rocks.

Remember the first disciples were fishermen, who would have been able to relate to what Jesus is saying here. So when we read “Be Careful,” Jesus is wanting to get our attention, he is saying that if we do not hear what he is going to say here, we are in danger of beaching our faith and shipwrecking our testimonies.

One of the ways we shipwreck our faith is sometimes we forget who we really are, we forget that we are children of the living God. Sometimes the storms of life cause us to hit the rocks and we feel that we have been ‘beached’ or stuck and we can’t move.

It is so easy to react to the storms of life by feeling that I must try harder, I must pray more, and I must read the bible more so I can get through this crisis. Spiritual disciplines are always a good thing. However in times of crisis we need more than spiritual disciplines and self effort, we need a fresh revelation of God.

Every commentary I have read on Matthew 6 believes that Jesus is teaching his disciples how to practice healthy wholesome Christian disciplines. So he talks about how they should give to the poor, how they should pray and how they should fast. Jesus is teaching how to cultivate a proper heart attitude so they can participate in the natural spiritual requirements of a follower of Jesus. The more I have looked at the chapter, the more I am inclined to think that the giving, praying and fasting, which are extremely important, are secondary issues as far as Matthew 6 is concerned. There is a much more important issue that is not often picked up.

If you read the whole Sermon on the Mount especially chapter 6 you will find one word that is repeated 17 times, 11 of which are in chapter 6. That word is Father. The word father is found more in Matthew 6 than any other chapter in the bible therefore it has a lot to teach us about God as our father, and what it means to be his child.

It’s really important to God that we have a revelation of what it means to have Him as our father. How we live and what we live for is determined by our understanding of the fatherhood of God and the security it produces in our lives.

Before we look at the chapter let us say a few things about God as our father.

In the Old Testament, the Jewish people had some kind of concept of God being a loving Father; however, this understanding of God was not often used. They saw God more as the Father of the nation, but not the individual.

When Jesus prayed he used the Aramaic word Abba for father. This is a word that was only used in the context of the home; it carried the idea on intimacy and respect. The Jews of Jesus’ time would have conversed in Aramaic or used Greek in everyday life, but they were trained to pray in classical Hebrew. The Jewish people at the time of Christ would have had a slight understanding of God as a loving and protective father, so it was not a completely new or alien concept to them, but they rarely addressed God as “Father” in prayer, which Jesus almost always did.

In biblical times a persons’ identity was always tied up with their father, e.g. when Jesus first met Simon He said, ‘You are Simon son of John, you shall be called Peter’. John 1.42. The designation ‘son of’ was like our surnames, it helped distinguish people who had the same first name.

J. I. Packer, in his book Knowing God says, "You sum up the whole of New Testament teaching in a single phrase, if you speak of it as a revelation of the Fatherhood of the holy Creator. In the same way, you sum up the whole of New Testament religion if you describe it as the knowledge of God as one's Holy Father. If you want to judge how well a person understands Christianity, find out how much he makes of the thought of being God's child, and having God as his Father. If this is not the thought that prompts and controls his worship and prayers and his whole outlook on life, it means that he does not understand Christianity very well at all." Citation: J. I. Packer, Knowing God, p. 182.
prayer: Father thank you that no matter the circumstances I am facing you are always a loving father.
